Panama Hit by Nationwide Strike, Disrupting Transport and Port Operations

PANAMA CITY, June 13 — A nationwide general strike that began on Thursday has brought economic activity to a near halt in Panama, with public transportation, port operations, and government services severely disrupted as thousands of workers joined walkouts across multiple sectors.

The strike, organized by a coalition of labor unions and civic groups, is the largest in Panama in over a decade. Protesters are demanding wage increases, greater job security, and changes to recent labor reforms they say threaten workers’ rights. As of Thursday afternoon, the action was still ongoing, with no signs of a breakthrough in talks between union leaders and government officials.

Major highways in and around Panama City were blocked by striking workers and supporters, causing lengthy traffic jams and leaving commuters stranded. Public buses operated at limited capacity, while several Metro stations reported partial closures due to staff shortages.

The country’s principal ports, including Balboa and Colón, reported work stoppages that delayed cargo loading and unloading. The National Chamber of Maritime Commerce said in a statement that port throughput had dropped by more than 60 percent since the early morning, warning that “extended disruptions could impact supply chains throughout the region.”

Flights at Tocumen International Airport operated normally, but airport ground staff staged a two-hour walkout in late morning, delaying some departures and arrivals. Customs processing at the border with Costa Rica was slowed, with freight trucks backed up for several kilometers.

“We cannot remain silent while our livelihoods are threatened,” said Luis Mena, spokesman for the United Workers Front, which represents transport and dock workers. “Unless the government listens to our demands, we will continue to take action.”

Government spokesperson Ana Rodríguez called for calm and urged union leaders to return to negotiations. “We respect the right to protest, but we also have a responsibility to keep the country running. We are open to dialogue and ready to address legitimate concerns,” Rodríguez said during a televised address.

Analysts estimate that the strike is costing Panama’s economy millions of dollars per day. “With the country’s strategic position as a regional logistics hub, even a short-lived shutdown can have serious ripple effects,” said Ricardo Guerra, an economist at the Panamerican Policy Institute.

The Panamanian Association of Retailers said many shops and supermarkets remained closed or operated with skeleton staff, citing difficulties in receiving shipments and concerns over possible unrest.

As the strike entered its second day, both union representatives and government officials signaled willingness to continue talks, but no agreement had been reached by late Thursday. Further demonstrations and road blockades were expected overnight.
